bodies.intuition: Generate many candidate answers and train a second model to say which one is right. It works for the same reason marking is easier than solving: checking a chain of reasoning is a different and usually simpler task than producing one, so a verifier can be smaller than the generator and still beat it at telling good from bad.
bodies.engineer: Best-of-n with a verifier reliably beats majority voting once n grows, because voting can only pick the modal answer while a verifier can pick a correct answer that only one sample found. The failure mode is the one every learned scorer has: optimise hard enough against the verifier and you find the answers it likes rather than the answers that are right, so the gains flatten and then reverse as n grows past where the verifier's judgement holds.
bodies.math: This is a detection problem, and the base rate is where it bites. If the generator is right one time in twenty, then even a verifier that accepts 90% of correct answers and 10% of wrong ones is picking a wrong answer more often than a right one — and the ranking that best-of-n depends on is only as good as that separation. Which is why verifier quality, not sample count, is what bounds the whole approach.
